981.title: The resentment list
981.howItsDone: In Alcoholics Anonymous, members often write a resentment inventory with a sponsor's help, listing whom they resent, why, and what it affected, and then looking at their own part.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the drafts folder letter. Your line was said, not sent. Is the page still in the drawer? Today, a different kind of writing: not one letter to one person, but a list. Day nine hundred eighty-one.

"He abused me, he beat me, he defeated me, he robbed me." That's not a police report. It's the third verse of the Dhammapada, the Buddhist collection of sayings, in Max Müller's translation. Read it again and it sounds like something the mind says at night, on a loop, about a boss or a sibling or an ex. A list, recited from memory, item by item. The verse isn't asking anyone to pretend the list is false. It's pointing at what happens to the one who keeps reciting it. Today: the resentment list.
screen: `HE ABUSED ME, HE ROBBED ME.` → `A LIST, ON A LOOP.` → `WHAT HAPPENS TO THE ONE WHO RECITES IT.`

segments.voice: First, the verse finishes its sentence. After the list it says: "in those who harbour such thoughts hatred will never cease." The next verse repeats the same list and says that in those who do not harbor such thoughts, hatred will cease. The list is identical in both verses. What changes is harboring: keeping it docked, tied up, fed and looked after. Second, why paper helps. A list in your head never ends, because the mind keeps adding and repeating. A list on paper has edges. You can see there are five things, not five hundred, and that some of them are old and small. Alcoholics Anonymous makes a written practice of this. Its Big Book describes writing resentments down: who you resent, and what happened, and what it touched in you. Then, the uncomfortable part, it asks the writer to look honestly at their own share, where there is one. Not to excuse anyone, but to see the whole picture. Third, a warning from the letter to the Hebrews: "lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you, and thereby many be defiled." A root works underground. You don't see it until it has spread. Writing the list is a way of digging it up into daylight, where it can be looked at instead of growing in the dark. Fourth, honesty. The list only works if it's true. Not the noble version. Write the petty ones too, the ones you'd be embarrassed to say aloud. Nobody grades it. The page can hold the same list the Dhammapada quotes, without the harboring.
screen: `HATRED WILL NEVER CEASE.` · `A LIST ON PAPER HAS EDGES.` · `A ROOT OF BITTERNESS.` · `WRITE THE PETTY ONES TOO.` · then, large: `ON PAPER.`

segments.voice: Take a pen and a page. Write three resentments, honestly, one per line. For each, a name or a place, and in a few words what happened. Then, beside each, write what it touched: my pride, my money, my safety, my sense of being loved. If you're willing, add one more note: was there any part of it that was mine? Don't argue with yourself. Just write. When the three are down, look at the page for a few breaths. Count the lines. Notice that there are three, and that they stop. The bell holds the time.
Big Book. Alcoholics Anonymous's book, which describes writing resentments down honestly, so they can be seen instead of recited. Today's word.
Your line: on paper. Today, when one of the three starts replaying, tell yourself it's on paper now, and go back to what you were doing. Day nine hundred eighty-one.

the list is the same; what changes is whether it's harbored.

options: leave it off; it's beneath you.
write it down with the others.

fork.reveal: the list only works if it's true. the petty ones loop in the head just as hard as the big ones.

what it means: grudges written down honestly, so they have edges and can be looked at instead of recited.

982.title: Forgiving parents
982.hook: forgiving parents, with honesty about what happened
982.howItsDone: Jews and Christians read the commandment to honor father and mother alongside the honest family stories of Genesis, and some teachers in both traditions distinguish honoring parents from approving everything they did.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Big Book's resentment list. Your line was on paper. Were any names on it from your own family? Today, the people none of us got to choose. Day nine hundred eighty-two.

Genesis does not flatter its families. One verse sets up a whole household's trouble in a single sentence: "And Isaac loved Esau, because he did eat of his venison: but Rebekah loved Jacob." A father with a favorite. A mother with a different favorite. Two boys growing up under one roof. There's no gentle editing, no line about how they did their best. The text just says it. That honesty is a good place to start a hard subject. Today: forgiving parents.
screen: `GENESIS DOESN'T FLATTER.` → `A FATHER'S FAVORITE, A MOTHER'S FAVORITE.` → `THE TEXT JUST SAYS IT.`

segments.voice: First, honesty about what happened. Forgiving a parent doesn't begin with excuses. It begins the way Genesis does, by naming it. Isaac loved Esau. Rebekah loved Jacob. The text doesn't soften it, and the story that follows, of tricks and a stolen blessing and a brother who has to flee, shows what it cost. Second, the pattern travels. Years later, Jacob has sons of his own. And Genesis says: "Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his children, because he was the son of his old age: and he made him a coat of many colours." Israel is Jacob's other name. The favored son becomes the father who plays favorites. The coat is the same wound, handed down in brighter cloth. Third, today's line. They were young too. A parent who hurts a child was once a child in someone else's house, learning love the way it was shown there. Jacob learned favoritism as the favorite. Seeing that doesn't make the hurt smaller. It makes the person who caused it more human, a link in a chain rather than a monster at the top of one. Fourth, honoring is not approving. The commandment says "Honour thy father and thy mother." Some Jewish and Christian teachers point out that the verse asks for honor, not for agreement, and not for pretending. And nothing in today's practice asks anyone to forgive abuse on a timetable, or to go back somewhere unsafe. Where real harm happened, forgiveness, if it comes, can come slowly and from a distance. Today is for something smaller.
screen: `ISAAC LOVED ESAU, REBEKAH LOVED JACOB.` · `THE FAVORITE BECOMES THE FATHER.` · `A LINK IN A CHAIN.` · `HONOR IS NOT APPROVAL.` · then, large: `THEY WERE YOUNG TOO.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe slowly. Bring to mind one parent, or whoever raised you. If that relationship holds deep harm, choose someone else, or simply rest in the breath; that's a full practice too. Otherwise, choose one small thing of theirs that still stings: a phrase they used, a missed game, a habit. Name it honestly. Then picture them young, before you, being taught by their own parents. Hold both at once: this happened, and they were young too. The bell holds the time.
Forgiving parents. Naming honestly what happened, and seeing the person who did it as someone who was once a child too. Today's word.
Your line: they were young too. Today, when that one small thing comes up, picture the young person they once were, and let the sting soften by one degree. Day nine hundred eighty-two.

myth: Genesis presents its families without faults
it says plainly that Isaac loved Esau and Rebekah loved Jacob, and shows what it cost.
the favored son Jacob grew up to play favorites himself
"Israel loved Joseph more than all his children."
seeing a parent as once young means saying the hurt was okay
it doesn't make the hurt smaller; it makes the person more human.

fork.setup: you're Jacob, grown up, the son your mother favored. now you have sons of your own. what do you do?
options: love them all the same, having learned your lesson.
favor one son, and give him a special coat.
favor the eldest, as custom expects.
fork.reveal: Genesis says Israel loved Joseph more than all his children and made him a coat of many colours. the pattern traveled.

trapdoor: what you thought: forgiving parents means saying they did their best.
what it means: naming honestly what happened, then seeing them as people who were once children too.
what a scholar hears: Genesis shows favoritism in two generations, Rebekah with Jacob, then Jacob, called Israel, with Joseph.

983.title: The dead
983.hook: you can forgive someone who has died
983.howItsDone: The Talmud describes going to the grave of someone you wronged and saying aloud, before others, that you wronged them; some people visit graves to speak to those they've lost, sometimes to settle what was left unsaid.

segments.voice: Yesterday, forgiving parents. Your line was they were young too. Did the small sting soften at all? Today, the people who can no longer hear an apology, or offer one. Day nine hundred eighty-three.

A phone still holds a voicemail from someone who has died. It's two years old. It's about nothing, a question about dinner. And underneath it sits an argument that was never settled, because there was supposed to be time. Now there isn't. The person who could apologize is gone, and so is the person who could hear one. It's easy to assume that means the door has closed. Some very old texts say otherwise. Today: the dead.
screen: `A VOICEMAIL ABOUT NOTHING.` → `AN ARGUMENT NEVER SETTLED.` → `IS THE DOOR CLOSED?`

segments.voice: First, a king who gets the news. In the second book of Samuel, King David's son Absalom has turned against him, raised an army, and driven his father out of Jerusalem. In the battle that follows, Absalom is killed. When the messenger arrives, David doesn't celebrate a victory. He goes up to a room over the gate and weeps: "O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! would God I had died for thee." A son who tried to take his father's throne, and the father's cry is his name, over and over. Whatever lay between them, David's love goes on speaking to his son after he is gone. Second, the other direction. The Talmud records a teaching for someone who wronged a person who has since died. They can't go and appease the person anymore, so the teaching says to bring others with them to the grave and say there, aloud, that they wronged this person. The relationship still carries weight after death. The words are still worth saying, in a place, with witnesses. Third, forgiving the dead. If an apology can be offered to the dead, forgiveness can be offered to them too. The other person doesn't need to take part. They never did. Forgiveness, as this whole block has been saying, happens in the one who forgives. Saying it out loud gives it a time and a place, so it isn't only a thought that comes and goes. Fourth, what it doesn't require. It doesn't require pretending they were someone else. David's son still rebelled. The wrong still happened. Forgiving the dead is releasing what you're still holding, not rewriting who they were. It still counts.
screen: `O MY SON ABSALOM.` · `WORDS SPOKEN AT THE GRAVE.` · `THEY DON'T NEED TO TAKE PART.` · `RELEASE, NOT REWRITE.` · then, large: `IT STILL COUNTS.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe slowly. Bring to mind someone who has died, with whom something was left unsettled. If that's too heavy today, choose something small, or simply sit with their memory. Picture them, as clearly as you can. Then, if you're somewhere you can, say aloud, quietly, what you forgive them for. One sentence is enough. If you're not alone, move your lips without sound. Then sit with whatever comes. If you pray, you can name them in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
The dead. Forgiveness, or an apology, offered to someone who has died, spoken in a time and place, even though they can't answer. Today's word.
Your line: it still counts. Today, if the unsettled thing comes back, remember you said it aloud, and that it still counts. Day nine hundred eighty-three.

what it means: forgiveness and apology can still be spoken, in a time and place, without a reply.

984.title: Angry with God
984.hook: Job and the psalmists were allowed to be angry with God (Psalm 22:1)
984.howItsDone: Jews and Christians pray the psalms of lament, including Psalm 22, and some teachers in both traditions point to Job and the lament psalms as a model for bringing anger and complaint honestly to God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the dead. Your line was it still counts. Did you say anything aloud? Today, the hardest place some people's anger goes: upward. Day nine hundred eighty-four.

"My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" Those are the first words of Psalm 22. Not a hymn of thanks. Not a calm reflection. A cry, aimed straight at God, asking why. It sits inside the Bible's own prayer book, kept and prayed. Somebody decided that this belonged in scripture, accusation and all. It wasn't filed away as an embarrassing moment or softened into something more polite. It was left exactly as raw as it is, for anyone who would ever need those words. Today: angry with God.
screen: `WHY HAST THOU FORSAKEN ME?` → `A CRY, NOT A HYMN.` → `KEPT IN THE PRAYER BOOK.`

segments.voice: First, the psalm keeps going. Psalm 22 goes on: "why art thou so far from helping me, and from the words of my roaring?" Roaring. Not whispering. The psalm does move, later, toward trust and praise, but it doesn't skip the roar to get there. The same opening line appears in another place too: in Matthew and Mark, Jesus cries it from the cross. Second, Job. Job loses his children, his wealth, his health, and his friends arrive with explanations. Job refuses them. He says: "I will not refrain my mouth; I will speak in the anguish of my spirit; I will complain in the bitterness of my soul." He spends chapter after chapter demanding that God answer him. Third, the surprise at the end. When God finally speaks, out of the whirlwind, Job is pressed hard with questions. But as the book closes, God's anger turns on the friends who defended God so neatly: "ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath." The one who complained is the one who spoke rightly. Readers differ about what exactly that means. One reading: honest anger, brought to God, counts as a kind of faithfulness. Pretending does not. Fourth, the prophet Habakkuk opens his book the same way: "O LORD, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear!" Again, it's kept, as scripture. Some people who pray hear these texts as a permission. For people who don't, there's still something here: the anger at how things went, at loss, at unfairness, is allowed to be said out loud, rather than buried. Honest is allowed.
screen: `THE WORDS OF MY ROARING.` · `I WILL NOT REFRAIN MY MOUTH.` · `JOB SPOKE RIGHTLY.` · `HOW LONG SHALL I CRY?` · then, large: `HONEST IS ALLOWED.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let the breath come and go. Find one honest complaint, something about your life that seems unfair, or a loss that never made sense. Don't tidy it. If God is part of your life, you can say it to God, plainly, the way the psalm does: why? If not, say it to life, or to the night sky, or just to the room. Say it once, aloud or under your breath. Then stay in the quiet that follows. Nothing has to answer. The bell holds the time.
Habakkuk. One of the prophets whose honest complaint, carried straight to God, scripture keeps rather than softens. Today's word.
Your line: honest is allowed. Today, when the polite version starts forming, in prayer or in conversation, try saying the true one instead. Day nine hundred eighty-four.

985.title: Forgiving institutions
985.hook: forgiving a church, a company, a country is different from forgiving a person
985.howItsDone: Jews and Christians read Daniel 9 as a model of confessing wrongs on behalf of a whole people, and some communities and institutions today issue collective apologies for past harms while victims decide for themselves whether and how to forgive.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Habakkuk, angry with God. Your line was honest is allowed. Did the true version get said anywhere? Today, anger aimed at something with no single face. Day nine hundred eighty-five.

A hospital billing office. A school that looked away. A congregation that closed ranks. A company that laid off a whole floor by email. A government office that lost the file, again. When the hurt comes from one of these, who exactly is there to forgive? The receptionist didn't write the policy. The pastor who's there now wasn't there then. The building can't apologize. There's no single person to sit across from. Today: forgiving institutions.
screen: `NO SINGLE FACE.` → `WHO WROTE THE POLICY?` → `THE BUILDING CAN'T APOLOGIZE.`

segments.voice: First, a prayer in the plural. In the book of Daniel, Daniel prays on behalf of his whole people: "We have sinned, and have committed iniquity, and have done wickedly, and have rebelled." We. Not I. Daniel names the kings, the princes and the fathers who came before him, and he still says we. In Daniel's prayer, wrong can belong to a group, not just to one person. Second, the trouble with forgiving a group. When a person hurts you, you can forgive that person. When an institution hurts you, the hurt is spread across a policy, a culture, many hands and a lot of silence. Forgiving it can feel like trying to hug fog. That's today's line: bigger than one. Third, a way through. Henry David Thoreau, in his essay on civil disobedience, observes that it's said a corporation has no conscience, but that a corporation of conscientious people has one. Institutions are made of people. Some find it possible to separate the two: to release bitterness toward the individuals inside, who may be doing their best, while still naming what the institution as a whole did. Fourth, forgiveness is not the same as dropping the matter. You can let go of the poison you carry about a church, a company or a country, and still write the letter, file the complaint, vote, or speak up so it doesn't happen to the next person. In Daniel, the confession and the plea for things to be put right come together, in the same breath. In this way of seeing it, the letting go is for the one who was hurt, and the accountability is for whoever comes next.
screen: `WE HAVE SINNED.` · `LIKE TRYING TO HUG FOG.` · `A CORPORATION WITH A CONSCIENCE.` · `RELEASE IT, STILL SPEAK UP.` · then, large: `BIGGER THAN ONE.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe slowly. Name one institution that has hurt you: a school, a workplace, a religious community, an agency, a system. Say its name silently. Notice where in your body the anger sits. Now picture one ordinary person inside it, someone who had nothing to do with what happened to you. See if you can let them off the hook, just them. Then, separately, name one thing you'd still want the institution to own or change. Both can stay true. The bell holds the time.
Forgiving institutions. Releasing bitterness toward a group with no single face, while still asking it to own what it did. Today's word.

Your line: bigger than one. Today, when you deal with that institution or one like it, be kind to the one person in front of you, and keep your honest complaint for the place it belongs. Day nine hundred eighty-five.

986.title: Boundaries after
986.hook: forgiveness and safety can go together
986.howItsDone: Some counselors, pastors and rabbis teach that forgiveness does not require trusting someone again right away, and point to Joseph's testing of his brothers in Genesis 42–45 as a story of forgiveness that waited to see change.

segments.voice: Yesterday, forgiving institutions. Your line was bigger than one. Were you kind to the one person in front of you? Today, the question that comes after forgiving anyone: then what? Day nine hundred eighty-six.

A woman forgives her brother for borrowing money and never paying it back. She means it. The bitterness is gone. A month later he calls, warm and friendly, and asks to borrow again. And here is the question that can trip people up: if she's really forgiven him, doesn't she have to say yes? Doesn't saying no mean she's still holding it against him? Genesis has a story about a man who tested the lock before he opened the door to his brothers. Today: boundaries after.
screen: `THE BITTERNESS IS GONE.` → `HE ASKS AGAIN.` → `DOES FORGIVING MEAN YES?`

segments.voice: First, Joseph. His brothers sold him into slavery. Years later, he's governor in Egypt, and in a famine the same brothers arrive to buy grain. They don't recognize him. He recognizes them. And he doesn't rush to embrace them. He tests them. He keeps one brother as a hostage, then frames the youngest, Benjamin, and watches what the others will do. Will they abandon this brother the way they abandoned him? Second, the answer. Judah, the brother who once suggested selling Joseph, steps forward and offers to stay as a slave in Benjamin's place. Only then does Joseph break down and say: "I am Joseph your brother, whom ye sold into Egypt." He weeps and kisses his brothers, but only after he has watched what they do. One way to read the testing: he waited until he'd seen whether they had changed before he let them close. Third, the wisdom books are practical about safety. Proverbs says: "Make no friendship with an angry man; and with a furious man thou shalt not go: Lest thou learn his ways, and get a snare to thy soul." That isn't hatred. It's caution. Some people are not safe to walk beside, and the texts don't ask anyone to pretend otherwise. Fourth, how the two fit. Forgiveness lives inside you: you let go of the debt, the bitterness, the replay. A boundary lives in what you do: what you lend, where you go, when you answer the phone. One doesn't cancel the other. The sister in the story can forgive her brother completely and still say: I'm not lending money again. That's not a grudge. That's a door with a lock. Forgive, and stay safe.
screen: `JOSEPH TESTS HIS BROTHERS.` · `WHOM YE SOLD INTO EGYPT.` · `WITH A FURIOUS MAN THOU SHALT NOT GO.` · `INSIDE, AND IN WHAT YOU DO.` · then, large: `FORGIVE AND STAY SAFE.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let the breath slow down. Bring to mind one person you've forgiven, or are trying to, where something still needs protecting: your time, your money, your peace, your body. Name the boundary in one plain sentence. I don't lend money anymore. I leave when the shouting starts. I don't answer after ten at night. Say it silently, without anger. Notice that you can wish them well and still keep it. If you pray, you can pray for them and for your own safety in the same breath. The bell holds the time.
Boundaries after. Letting go of the bitterness inside, while still protecting what needs protecting in what you do. Today's word.
Your line: forgive and stay safe. Today, keep one boundary you named, kindly and without apology, and notice that the forgiveness is still there. Day nine hundred eighty-six.

987.title: Forgiving strangers
987.hook: the driver who cut in, the rude clerk
987.howItsDone: Jews and Christians read Proverbs and Ecclesiastes among the Bible's wisdom books; Proverbs 19:11, on passing over an offense, is sometimes quoted when people talk about letting small slights go.

segments.voice: Yesterday, boundaries after. Your line was forgive and stay safe. Which limit did you keep? This week we wrote lists, faced parents, the dead, God, and whole institutions. Today the smallest hurts of all, from people we'll never see again. Day nine hundred eighty-seven.

The light turns green, and a gray hatchback slides into the lane with no signal, close enough to touch. A horn goes off. Later, at the pharmacy counter, the clerk sighs, doesn't look up, and pushes the bag across without a word. Neither of them knows your name. Neither will ever think of you again. And yet these two can follow someone around for a whole afternoon, retold at dinner, replayed in the shower. The big hurts get the long weeks of this path. Today belongs to the small ones, the strangers. Two short sayings from the Bible's wisdom books have a plan for them.
screen: `NO SIGNAL. NO LOOK.` → `TWO STRANGERS, ONE AFTERNOON.` → `TWO OLD SAYINGS.`

segments.voice: First, a proverb. Proverbs nineteen says, in the King James words: "The discretion of a man deferreth his anger; and it is his glory to pass over a transgression." Deferreth: puts off, slows down. The anger isn't banned. It's made to wait, long enough for good sense to catch up. Second, the verb. Pass over. Not punish, not report, not retell at dinner. The picture is of walking past something on the road, the way the gray hatchback is already three blocks away. And the proverb doesn't call this weakness. It calls it glory. Third, a mirror, from Ecclesiastes. It advises against straining to hear every word said about you, or you may hear your own servant cursing you. Then it gives the reason: "For oftentimes also thine own heart knoweth that thou thyself likewise hast cursed others." The clerk is having a day. So have you, and on some of those days someone else was the stranger on the receiving end. Today's line is a short way of remembering both. Fourth, quick isn't the same as fake. Cutting someone off is still dangerous. Rudeness is still rude. Passing over it just means not carrying a stranger home. They were a stranger at breakfast. They don't need to become a roommate in your head by dinner.
screen: `ANGER, MADE TO WAIT.` · `PASS OVER IT.` · `YOU'VE HAD DAYS TOO.` · `DON'T CARRY THEM HOME.` · then, large: `THEY'RE HAVING A DAY.`

segments.voice: Settle in and let the breath slow. Bring back one stranger from the last few days: a driver, a caller, someone in a line. See the moment clearly, just once. Then let the picture widen. They woke up somewhere this morning. They have a kitchen, a phone full of messages, a problem you know nothing about. You don't have to like what they did. Just let them be a whole person with a whole day. On an out-breath, let them go back to that day, without you. If they come back, send them off again. If you pray, you can include that stranger in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Forgiving strangers. Letting go quickly of small hurts from people you'll never meet again, without pretending they were fine. Today's word.
Your line: they're having a day. The next time a stranger is rude, say the line silently, and see how quickly you can let them drive on. Day nine hundred eighty-seven.

match.prompt: two old sayings — tap the pairs.

myth: Proverbs calls passing over an offense a weakness
"it is his glory to pass over a transgression."
Ecclesiastes reminds its reader that they have cursed others too
"thine own heart knoweth that thou thyself likewise hast cursed others."
forgiving a stranger quickly means the rudeness was fine
it was still rude; passing over it just means not carrying it home.

fork.setup: a stranger snaps at you in a line. you could answer back, report them, or do something else. what does Proverbs 19:11 call glory?
options: answering back, so they learn.
passing over it.
remembering it, to tell later.
fork.reveal: "it is his glory to pass over a transgression." the anger is deferred, made to wait, and the offense is walked past.

original.note: Hebrew, Proverbs 19:11: to pass over, to go by or across.

trapdoor: what you thought: forgiving strangers means being a pushover.
what it means: letting the anger wait, remembering your own bad days, and not carrying the stranger home.
what a scholar hears: Proverbs 19:11 uses avor, an everyday Hebrew verb for passing by or crossing over, so the offense is pictured as something you walk past.
